Chilean spies reported the departure, and the Chilean combat fleet turned to face the enemy; the order was given that there would be no more training exercises—if the call to battle stations sounded, it meant the Argentine fleet was right in front of them. After advancing for a few hours toward the Drake Passage and Cape Horn, the Chilean fleet received news that the Argentine fleet had turned around and was heading back to its anchorages! comments.author: @Yucaste
comments.text:
When major nations gave up on rescuing Shackleton's men, he traveled to Punta Arenas, Chile—on the Strait of Magellan—where Pilot Pardo agreed to undertake the rescue mission aboard his small cutter, the *Yelcho*. Before setting sail, he wrote to his father: "If I fail and die, you will have to look after my Laura and my children, who will be left without any means of support. If I succeed, I will have fulfilled my humanitarian duty and my duty as a Chilean. By the time you read this letter, your son will either be dead or will have arrived in Punta Arenas. I will not return alone. Although the mission is difficult, risky, and fraught with danger, I have not hesitated to accept it—among other reasons—because it is a humanitarian one."
The *Escampavía Yelcho* was a Chilean Navy patrol vessel commanded by Pilot Pardo; it became famous for rescuing the survivors of the ill-fated Shackleton expedition in 1916.

The rescue: On August 30, 1916, after crossing the treacherous Drake Passage and navigating through Antarctic ice, he successfully rescued all members of the British expedition without a single casualty.
Recognition: Following the feat, the British government offered him a substantial financial reward, which Pardo declined, stating that he had merely fulfilled his duty as a sailor.

Two Chilean Navy ships have borne the name "Piloto Pardo":
• AP-45 *Piloto Pardo*: An Antarctic transport and service vessel acquired in 1959 and in service for 38 years.
• OPV-81 *Piloto Pardo*: A Chilean Navy offshore patrol vessel currently in service, specializing in surveillance and rescue operations in southern Chile.

comments.text:
It is worth remembering that what is commonly called “Drake’s Passage” is more properly known by its original Spanish name, Mar de Hoces (Sea of Hoces). The passage was crossed in 1526 by Francisco de Hoces, more than half a century before Francis Drake’s voyage through the region.

It is remarkable how historical naming can overshadow the earlier explorers who actually made the discovery. Hoces’s name was largely lost from international usage, while Drake’s became attached to the passage, reflecting how European exploration was often recorded and remembered in later English-language sources.

Perhaps it is time to recognize the historical record and give Francisco de Hoces and the Mar de Hoces the recognition they deserve.
